en: Rainwater dissolves the coral limestone of the Chocolate Hills, leaving behind isolated, cone-shaped mounds of grass-covered earth.
When cold lake water touches Taal Volcano's hot magma, it flashes into steam, causing explosive steam-driven eruptions.
Slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolves the limestone bedrock of Palawan, carving out the massive Puerto Princesa Subterranean River cave.
Habagat winds pick up moisture from the West Philippine Sea, dropping heavy rainfall across western Luzon during summer.
Magma beneath Albay heats underground water into high-pressure steam, which spins turbines to generate electricity at the Tiwi Geothermal Power Plant.
The stepped walls of the Banaue Rice Terraces slow down mountain water runoff, preventing severe soil erosion on steep slopes.
Abnormally warm ocean temperatures cause Tubbataha Reef corals to expel their colorful algae, turning the reefs stark white.
High tides from Manila Bay push saltwater upstream, temporarily reversing the freshwater flow of the Pasig River.
Thick, sticky lava from Mayon Volcano cools quickly near the vent, piling up to form its perfectly symmetrical cone shape.
The towering Sierra Madre mountain range forces moisture-laden typhoons to rise and drop their rain on the eastern coast.
Soil washed from deforested upland areas settles at the bottom of Laguna de Bay, gradually making the lake shallower.
The Eurasian plate sinks beneath the Philippine Sea plate at the Philippine Trench, melting rock to fuel local volcanoes.
